summary:
Katsina State stands under the national framework of Nigeria: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies nationwide and reaches beyond marriage, banning cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that police have used the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Katsina adds a second, religious criminal layer. Human Rights Watch (2004) documents the spread of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria and lists twelve states concerned: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, a process traced from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000. The provisions cited remain in force. Katsina's own instrument is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, which came into operation on 20 June 2001 and was gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23 of 27 August 2001.

The penalties in Katsina are the most severe recorded anywhere in the country for same-sex acts between women. Ostien's annotated volume places Katsina among the three states, with Kaduna and Kebbi, whose sodomy text reads that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm). Footnote 183 of the same volume shows that only Kano and Katsina reach stoning to death as the maximum for the lesbianism offence, against the harmonised code's base of 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment. Katsina is therefore one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum penalty for same-sex acts between women as well as between men. The UK Home Office note confirms that Sharia law in all twelve states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Gender expression carries its own exposure. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Nigeria' records a cross-dressing layer in which men who dress or behave as women face prison or a fine, citing a 20 June 2025 Kano court sentence of a TikToker to one year in prison over a cross-dressing video. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute.

Violence against trans people is documented at national level with official indifference following. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Police violence against perceived gay people is routine: TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Prison placement for a trans detainee in Katsina is governed by discretion rather than any published rule. The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), who pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, and served it in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Practical safety in Katsina rests on the wider pattern rather than a locally documented record: no court-case study samples this state, no religious-police operation is documented for it, and no trans-specific incident is on record. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Katsina's sodomy provision is not unique in its severity but its lesbianism provision is: three states (Katsina, Kaduna, Kebbi) prescribe stoning to death for sodomy, while only Kano and Katsina extend the death penalty to same-sex acts between women. The harmonised northern code sets a far lower base of 50 lashes and up to six months, so the Katsina text sits well above the regional norm.

The cross-dressing offence has produced a custodial sentence in a neighbouring state: a Kano court sentenced a TikToker to one year in prison on 20 June 2025 over a cross-dressing video. That is the closest documented prosecution to Katsina and indicates how the offence is being used in practice.

Arrest and prosecution data for sexual orientation and gender identity offences is limited in Nigeria, according to the UK Home Office note, so the frequency of enforcement cannot be established from these sources. The absence of a Katsina case study therefore reflects the state of the record rather than an absence of enforcement.

Nigeria's hybrid legal system means a visitor in Katsina is exposed to two overlapping criminal regimes at once: the secular SSMPA with its 10 to 14-year penalties, and the state Sharia code with corporal and capital punishment. The UK Home Office note documents the 12-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women.
localsOnly:
Katsina's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 (Law No. 2 of 2001) has been in operation since 20 June 2001 and was gazetted on 27 August 2001; residents live under it continuously, and the June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force.

Residents convicted of sodomy face stoning to death (rajm) under the Katsina text, and the lesbianism offence carries a maximum of stoning to death against a harmonised base of 50 lashes and up to six months. Men who dress or behave as women face prison or a fine under the cross-dressing layer.

Nothing in the sources sets out a housing rule, segregation policy, women's-wing arrangement or any other prison-administration measure for Katsina. Placement of a trans detainee between male and female sections is therefore not governed by any published Katsina-specific rule in this record.

Police conduct in the wider country includes extortion and beating of men perceived as gay, and the SSMPA is described by those affected as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text. No Katsina-specific police operation is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted at national level is not settled by the sources available here. The cross-dressing penalty described for Katsina's neighbouring states derives from Wikipedia's account of state-level practice, not from a Katsina statute cited in this inventory.

Unresolved: no source in this inventory states a housing, segregation or placement rule for trans prisoners in Katsina. Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Nigeria' contains nothing for Katsina on this point, and the global overview article on LGBTQ people in prison returns zero mentions of Nigeria or Nigerians on a full-text scan, so it documents no Nigeria- or Katsina-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, special unit or segregation-for-placement practice. That is negative evidence, not a finding that no policy exists.

Unresolved: no court-case study samples Katsina and no religious-police operation is documented for it, so the enforcement picture here is inferred from the twelve-state pattern rather than observed locally. Arrest and prosecution data for these offences is limited nationwide, per the UK Home Office note.

Unresolved: no trans-specific violent incident is on record for Katsina. The documented killings, police beatings and app-based extortion cited here occurred in Abuja and Lagos and are reported as national context.
